extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; general educated public interested in lectures on great authors and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century lecture on the nature and qualities of 'Great Men' (Poet, Prophet, Priest, Reformer) emphasizing how to recognise greatness in writers such as Shakespeare, Dante and reformers like Luther and Knox. Focuses on intellectual, moral and aesthetic criteria for evaluating such figures and their works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of vision / 'seeing eye'
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty to discern the inner heart, generic secret, and true structure of things; the power to find beginnings, sequences and endings and to make order out of chaos ('Fiat lux').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasised as the poet's first gift and the best measure of intellect: 'To the Poet... See.' Examples: Shakespeare's ability to fashion narratives from raw dramatic materials and to discern what must be suppressed or made prominent. Anti-pattern: mere stringing of rhymes without insight; jingling sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: An overall intellectual superiority that unifies imagination, fancy and understanding — the decisive quality in a great man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the principal thing to say about Shakespeare: an 'unconscious intellect' that comprehends whole situations calmly and deeply. Compared favorably to Bacon's Novum Organum; marks capacity for deliberate illumination of subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative perspicacity / portrait-painting of men
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity to delineate characters and men fully and generically so they reveal both outward traits and inward mechanism ('characters are like watches... the inward mechanism also is all visible').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare praised for setting forth complete, sympathetic portraits (Falstaff, Othello, Juliet, Coriolanus). This criterion values truthful, comprehensive character-delineation rather than caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality as prerequisite to true knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge requires a moral relation to the object; without justice, courage and virtuous sympathy a man cannot truly know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: intellect and moral nature are not separable; a thoroughly immoral man cannot comprehend truth. Example/analogy: the Fox knows where geese lodge only because of vulpine practical virtues. Anti-pattern: selfish, 'eye-servant' behavior that produces dishonest or superficial work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / unconscious growth from Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic worth arises from works growing unconsciously from the deep nature of the artist rather than from artifice or conscious contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare's art is praised as 'not Artifice' but emerging from 'the deeps of Nature' in the artist. Works that feel contrived score lower; those that reveal new harmonies to later generations score higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / perennial truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of a work or author to address the noble, pure and great for all times and places; to be recognised as 'true' wherever an open human soul exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare and Dante held up as voices with universal, enduring appeal; such works will survive across ages and cultures. Guidance: evaluate whether passages 'spoken once and forever' resonate beyond their era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner harmony with Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceiving and expressing the 'musical idea' or inner harmony that dwells in phenomena so that disparate embodiments cohere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'seeing eye' discerns what Nature meant and unwraps hidden beauty. Works that exhibit natural symmetry and conformity to 'Truth' exemplify this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit of means to materials / adaptation to conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist's skill in translating thought into the media and materials available; making the thought fit the 'stone' or stage provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare's plays are shaped by the Globe Playhouse constraints; greatness includes how well an artist works within actual conditions. 'Disjecta membra' may be inevitable; judge both flashes of radiance and surrounding conventional matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / lack of idolatrous self-assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: An authentic, sincere relation to subject-matter and people rather than arrogance, fanaticism, or conscious claim to prophetic status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for Shakespeare's lack of doctrinal self-assertion ('not a Sceptic' nor a conscious Prophet). Anti-pattern: figures who claim prophetic infallibility (comparison to Mahomet) whose conscious claims produce error and intolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to unify and give voice to a people
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a writer becomes an articulate, rallying voice that helps bind a nation or cultural community together across distance and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare presented as a 'King' that unites Englishmen globally; similar value as a national emblem surpassing political institutions. Example: Dante making Italy 'one' through voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of tragic depth and genial laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to encompass deep suffering and tragedy while retaining a genial, sympathetic capacity for laughter that never mocks misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare's mirthfulness is praised as 'genial laughter' not directed at poverty or helplessness; laughter indicates sympathy. Works should show humane laughter alongside tragic insight (Hamlet, Macbeth, Coriolanus vs Dogberry/Verges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic / Priestly function (spiritual leadership)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Priests/Reformers: being a 'voice from the unseen Heaven' who interprets spiritual significance to people and unites them in worship or reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luther and Knox are discussed as historical Priests/Reformers; criterion evaluates whether a figure appeals to invisible justice and guides communal life. The reformer as priest appeals to divine truth in opposition to worldly force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical rootedness and necessity of reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness that historical epochs change and that some great works or systems become obsolete, necessitating reform — originality and the ability to cause or respond to epochal change are signs of greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how Dante's Catholicism could be true in its epoch yet fail in another; the great man may be product of his time but also a catalyst for necessary change. Evaluate originality and capacity to precipitate or embody epochal shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure beyond outward effect (intrinsic worth over utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work or man should be judged by intrinsic spiritual, intellectual, and artistic quality rather than by worldly influence, political success or measurable 'effect on the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that influence/utility are not the real fruit of a man's work: Mahomet's worldly power is contrasted with Dante's narrower but nobler possession. Anti-pattern: equating utility or political success with ultimate greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to reveal concealed depths (rootedness and silence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of hidden sorrows, unconscious forces, and silent roots in a creator's work that suggest deeper life beneath surface utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare's Sonnets and dramatic tragedies testify to personal suffering and subterranean forces; 'Speech is great; but Silence is greater.' Evaluate whether works hint at deeper unseen origins rather than only surface brilliance.
